summary: Explains the rules and procedures for using compression (RFC 3274) inside an Internet EDI AS message, as defined by RFC 3335, RFC 4130 and RFC 4823. This is an informational document.

eli5.summary: Business documents sent between computers can be squished smaller, like packing a suitcase. This explains how to squish and unsquish them.

subtitle: How to shrink business documents inside EDI messages and calculate integrity checks correctly

tldr.problem: EDI (Electronic Data Interchange) messages sent over the Internet can be large and expensive to transmit, and there was no standardized way to compress them within the message structure.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3274 provides a compression layer that wraps messages using ZLIB compression inside a standard MIME format (application/pkcs7-mime). The compression can be applied at different layers depending on whether the message is signed or encrypted, and integrity checks (MIC) must be calculated consistently with the RFC 3335, 4130, and 4823 specifications.
tldr.outcome: EDI messages can now be compressed transparently, reducing bandwidth, and all implementations can follow consistent rules for computing integrity receipts and handling decompression errors.

today: RFC 5402 is an informational document that standardizes compression use in EDI messages. It remains the authoritative guide for AS2 and AS3 implementations that need to handle compressed payloads and correctly compute integrity checks for them.

sections.title: Compression for Business Documents
sections.content:
EDI (Electronic Data Interchange) is the standard way businesses exchange structured documents like invoices and purchase orders over the Internet. The EDIINT (EDIINT over the Internet) working group defined three main protocols: AS1 (email-based), AS2 (HTTP-based), and AS3 (FTP-based). Historically, these protocols had no standard, transport-neutral way to compress large payloads, even though businesses often need to exchange large documents and want to minimize bandwidth.

RFC 3274 introduced a compressed-data MIME type using ZLIB compression, making it possible to add a compression layer to any message without changing the transport protocol. However, adding compression to the layering rules for EDI messages (which can have payload, signature, and encryption layers) required new procedures for both construction and integrity verification. This document provides those procedures, explaining when and how to apply compression and how to correctly compute the Message Integrity Check (MIC) values that receivers return in Message Disposition Notifications (MDN).
sections.eli5: Business documents can be compressed to save space, but you need to know where to squish them (before or after signing) and how to check that unsquishing works right.

sections.title: Compression Layer Structure
sections.content:
The compressed-data layer is a MIME entity with Content-Type application/pkcs7-mime containing a CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) compressed-data object. Inside it sits the original business document (which could be XML, EDI text, or any other MIME type) that has been compressed using ZLIB (a deflate-based compression algorithm).

EDI 'AS' messages are multi-layered MIME structures. A typical message may have a payload layer (the business document), optionally a signature layer (proving who sent it), and optionally an encryption layer (keeping it private). Compression can be inserted at two different points: before signing (so the signed data includes compressed content) or after signing (so the entire signed message is compressed). The document specifies that you MUST NOT compress at both points in the same message. A receiver MUST support both approaches when unpacking inbound compressed documents, since either approach is valid.
sections.eli5: Squishing can happen before signing (making the signature cover compressed data) or after signing (squishing the whole thing). You can do one but not both.

sections.title: Six Message Structure Patterns
sections.content:
The document shows six layer combinations: unsigned/unencrypted compressed (3.1), signed/unencrypted with payload compressed before signing (3.2), signed/unencrypted with the entire signed structure compressed (3.3), unsigned/encrypted with payload compressed before encryption (3.4), signed/encrypted with payload compressed before signing and then encrypted (3.5), and signed/encrypted with the signed structure compressed before encryption (3.6). Each section diagrams the layer order and clarifies where MIME headers apply.

For example, in pattern 3.2 (signed/unencrypted/inner compress): the base MIME message contains a multipart/signed structure. Inside that, before the signature part, sits the compressed-data MIME entity wrapping the original business document. The receiver verifies the signature over the multipart body (which includes the compressed data), then decompresses the payload. In pattern 3.3 (signed/unencrypted/outer compress): the entire multipart/signed structure is compressed inside an application/pkcs7-mime entity. The receiver decompresses first, verifies the signature, then extracts the payload. These different approaches affect how MIC values are calculated.
sections.eli5: You can squish the document before signing, or squish the whole signed package. Similarly for encryption. The RFC shows six valid combinations and how to layer them.

sections.title: Integrity Checks for Compressed Messages
sections.content:
A Message Integrity Check (MIC) is a cryptographic fingerprint of the message content that the receiver computes and returns to the sender in an MDN, proving the message was not corrupted in transit. The MIC calculation rules differ based on the message type.

For signed messages, the MIC is computed over the same data that was signed: the MIME bodypart containing either the compressed or uncompressed payload. For encrypted/unsigned messages, the MIC is computed over the uncompressed data content, including MIME headers and any Content-Transfer-Encoding applied. For unsigned/unencrypted messages, the MIC is also computed over the uncompressed data with headers and encoding. In all cases, compression is transparent: the receiver decompresses, then calculates the MIC over the result. This ensures that two parties exchanging the same document (one compressed, one not) will compute identical MIC values.
sections.eli5: The integrity check is computed on the unsquished data so the sender and receiver always agree, no matter whether they compressed it.
